query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidizing cast HfNbTaTiZr in a low-partial-pressure O2 atmosphere at about 800–900 °C for 1–2 hours will form a stable, adherent oxide scale that substantially reduces oxygen ingress during subsequent exposure to air at 1000 °C without degrading the alloy’s characteristic ductility (8–16% at room temperature) or long-term yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the as-cast condition, exhibiting 8–16% RT tensile ductility, yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, and poor oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment in low-partial-pressure oxygen at 800–900 °C for 1–2 hours to create a thin oxide barrier layer on the as-cast alloy.
generation.conditions: Subsequent service in air at up to 1000 °C for 10–100 hours, under tensile strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1.
generation.structural_mediator: A stable, adherent oxide scale formed from constituent elements of HfNbTaTiZr, offering improved oxidation resistance.
generation.mechanism: By producing a superficial oxide film that resists further oxidation kinetics, the alloy experiences reduced oxygen pickup and preserves its high-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Sustained mechanical performance (8–16% RT elongation; 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C) with significantly improved oxidation resistance compared to untreated HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr exposed to the same conditions lacks a protective film, suffers embrittlement, and loses mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: Effective up to 1000 °C in air for durations of at least 10–100 hours, under strain rates from 10−4 to 10−2 s−1.
generation.uncertainty: Scale integrity may degrade under thermal cycles or overly prolonged exposures; the optimum pre-oxidation temperature–time profile requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set subjected to the pre-oxidation treatment, the other left untreated. Expose both sets in air at 1000 °C for 10–100 h under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1.
measurements: Mass gain and oxide layer thickness to assess oxygen uptake.
In situ tension tests to measure yield strength and ductility at elevated temperature.
Cross-sectional microscopy to investigate oxide scale uniformity and substrate integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain (or oxide scale growth) compared to untreated samples, or if their high-temperature strength and ductility do not match the baseline targets of 8–16% ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. decision.trend: Across these studies on HfNbTaTiZr or closely related refractory high-entropy alloys, researchers varied certain constituent elements (e.g., substituting Mo or V, partially removing Hf or Ta) or introduced interstitials (e.g., oxygen, nitrogen) to explore mechanical response at various temperatures. Such changes effectively tuned strength and ductility but did not resolve oxidation concerns. While good high-temperature yield strength and moderate ductility have been reported, oxidation resistance has remained a persistent gap, as the inherent reactivity of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr with oxygen leads to embrittlement and material loss under oxidizing conditions.
decision.unsolved: A robust method to suppress external oxygen ingress and scale growth at and above 1000 °C—without resorting to bulk composition shifts—has yet to be devised, leaving current RHEAs susceptible to premature failure in oxidizing environments.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to form a thin, adherent, stable oxide scale. For instance, hold the as-cast HfNbTaTiZr in a low-partial-pressure O2 atmosphere at ~800–900 °C for 1–2 h until a continuous barrier layer forms. In subsequent service at up to 1000 °C in air (for durations of at least 10–100 h) and under tensile strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, this engineered oxide film is hypothesized to impede oxygen ingress without significantly degrading the alloy’s 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility or its 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
decision.why: Trends in prior work show that altering bulk composition to improve oxidation resistance often compromises the alloy’s strength–ductility balance. However, forming a protective superficial oxide scale via a tailored pre-oxidation process avoids global composition changes. Such surface engineering strategies are commonly applied to superalloys for high-temperature applications. Here, a controlled environment ensures formation of an adherent, stable oxide from the existing constituent elements. Prior evidence from related RHEAs suggests that partial oxidation can create thin, protective layers at elevated temperatures. A falsification experiment would compare coupon samples with and without the pre-oxidized layer after isothermal exposure at 1000 °C over 10–100 h under 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ tensile loading in air, measuring mass gain, oxide spallation, and mechanical properties to confirm the hypothesized improvement in oxygen resistance and mechanical retention.
